catalog_quote: Golo, though originally a monosyllabic language like most languages in the B. G. P., may be said to have reached at present the stage of a bisyllabic language. A particular character of this bisyllabism is that the vowels are usually the same in both syllables. [p. 907] ... In fact, e and o always sound open, i. e., ɛ and ɔ in monosyllables. In bisyllables they sound open in the first accented syllable; they sound less open in the second unaccented syllable. But if any one is asked to pronounce a word slowly, syllable by syllable, all the e's and o's will sound open, i. e., like ɛ and ɔ. [pp. 907-908] ... Tones do not play such an important part in Golo as they do in Ndogo and related dialects. ... Therefore we shall not usually mark word-tones. new_statements.quote: In fact, e and o always sound open, i. e., ɛ and ɔ in monosyllables. In bisyllables they sound open in the first accented syllable; they sound less open in the second unaccented syllable. [p. 907] ... Tones do not play such an important part in Golo as they do in Ndogo and related dialects. [...] Therefore we shall not usually mark word-tones. We shall mark tones in cases in which "tone" alone gives the clue to a clear pronunciation and avoids misunderstandings. For the marking of tones, we follow the commonly adopted method, viz., "grave accent" for the "low tone", "acute accent" for the high tone, and no mark at all for the mid-tone. Other tones are not found in Golo. [p. 912]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Golo is a three-tone language (low, high, mid; tone is lexically contrastive but 'less important' than in Ndogo). The only prominence statement is incidental: in disyllabic words (the dominant word shape, usually with the same vowel in both syllables) the first syllable is 'accented' and the second 'unaccented', shown by fuller (more open) e/o in the first syllable. Provisional reading: initial accent in disyllables, alongside lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None for accent. For tone: 'a good number of words differing from each other only in tone' (e.g. dog vs goat, p. 911); p. 908 notes closed e/o arise from contraction (undè 'to help', ngie 'chief') as exceptions to the open-vowel rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated bisyllabic words in the vowel discussion); no phrase-level statement. The remark is made about vowel quality, not as a stress rule, and covers bisyllables only; longer words are not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Santandrea 1957 describes exactly Glottolog's golo1234: the Golo of the Bahr el Ghazal Province, Sudan (dialect groups K = Kayango, A/AE = Abushakka, N = Ngolemgbo), a Bandaic language distinct from Ndogo; Glottolog's own bib entry codes it 'Golo [NOCODE_Golo]'. Do not confuse with en.wikipedia 'Golo language', which redirects to West Banda [bbp, west2458] in the Central African Republic. Golo was already fully bilingual in Ndogo in the 1950s and is AES 'shifting'; there is no modern description.

sources.locator: II. Phonetics, §2 Vowels, p. 907 (accented syllable); §6 Tones, p. 912 (tone system). PDF pages 965 and 970 of; pages 11 and 16 of the extracted article PDF.
sources.note: No stress section. §II.2 Vowels (p. 907): in bisyllables e/o 'sound open in the first accented syllable; they sound less open in the second unaccented syllable'. §II.6 Tones (p. 912): three tones (low, high, mid; 'Other tones are not found in Golo'); tones 'do not play such an important part in Golo as they do in Ndogo'; word tones normally left unmarked but minimal pairs exist (dog/goat p. 911). Also p. 907: Golo 'originally a monosyllabic language' now largely bisyllabic, with the same vowel in both syllables.
